title: Why write code in 2026
description: Hacker News discussion on the role of manual coding in 2026. Covers debates on whether developers should still write code manually or rely entirely on AI agents. Key themes include: (1) Writing code helps build mental models and understanding - if you can't write code, you can't review it effectively. (2) Claude's hourly rate is ~$17, comparable to some human workers, but may rise as human engineers are 'Ubered away'. (3) LLMs can write complex code like Prolog interpreters in WebAssembly successfully. (4) AI tools compress development timelines but don't eliminate the need for developers who understand fundamentals. (5) The distinction between 'software prompters' who use AI for everything vs developers who use AI as a tool.
author: softwaredoug (author), HN community

title: Coding agents have replaced every framework I used
description: Hacker News discussion on replacing frameworks with AI-generated code. Key insights: (1) AWS demo at re:Invent showed SRE agents autonomously detecting, triaging, and fixing bugs in 2 minutes. (2) Debate over whether agents can maintain complex systems without human understanding of 'mental models'. (3) Concern about 'vibe coding' leading to unmaintainable codebases when AI hits limitations. (4) AI productivity gains: some report 10x improvements, others minimal benefit. (5) Frameworks provide shared mental models and patterns that AI-generated bespoke code lacks. (6) Real-world experiment: team used prompts to replace legacy system but abandoned it after months due to complexity and token costs. (7) Determinism argument: compilers are deterministic, LLMs are not - you can't reliably verify AI code without understanding it.
author: alainrk (author), HN community

title: AI Coding Agents: Adoption Trends - The JetBrains Blog
description: JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026 findings on AI coding agent adoption. Key insights: (1) 90% of professional developers use AI coding agents at least weekly, with 68% using them daily. (2) Claude Code has become the most widely adopted tool at 39% of developers (up from 18% in January 2026), with 47% adoption in the US. (3) Claude Code has a 31% 'main tool' rate, indicating ~80% conversion from usage to primary tool. (4) Codex adoption grew 5x from 3% to 16%, with awareness jumping from 27% to 65%. (5) GitHub Copilot lost leadership, declining from 29% to 21% adoption. (6) Cursor declined from 18% to 12%, with significant drop in China (28% to 16%). (7) OpenCode reached 7% adoption with 42% mindshare despite no big company backing. (8) JetBrains AI adoption at 9%, with Claude Agent, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and OpenCode integrated into JetBrains IDEs.
author: Mikhail Bogdanov, JetBrains Research
